extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists and students of fiction; readers seeking practical advice on writing novels
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance for composing fiction: what to aim for in plot, character, tone, and moral handling, plus career/practical advice for aspiring novelists. Emphasises observation, truth, pleasing the reader, and social responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public trust in established reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers naturally trust established names; a novel by a known author will be more readily read than the same work by an unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope compares this to buying from Fortnum & Mason or recognizing a Titian. He warns that new authors face slowness of public judgment and that reputation is earned by time and consistent quality; this influences how easily a writer's work finds an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware the limits of external judgment about talent
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice from others about whether you should pursue writing is often imperfect; certainty about who will succeed is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics or friends may counsel harshly or softly (e.g. 'darn your stockings' or 'try some other work'); such judgments can be mistaken (Byron's early verses example). One should recognize the fallibility of critics' forecasts and that it is rarely possible to be sure who will ultimately succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on literature as sole livelihood at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: If you must earn a living, do not begin by trusting to writing alone; secure stable income and write in spare hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope advises taking the 'stool in the office' or other steady employment while pursuing fiction in leisure hours. He cites his own ten years of insufficient earnings and the protection this approach gives if literary attempts fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept severe toil and perseverance as necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful writing often requires extended, severe labour and perseverance through failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends double toil (employment plus literary work) and notes many successful writers failed multiple times before succeeding. Perseverance is framed as required if one truly wants a literary career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write because you have a story to tell (not because you must produce)
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin a novel only when you truly have a series of events or development of character that you feel compelled to present, not merely to produce another book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope distinguishes the first novel ('have a story to tell') from later works written out of habit or obligation. Anti-pattern: writing from duty leads to 'woodenness' where characters are 'cut out of blocks' and incidents feel mechanical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain continuous observation and receptivity to life
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist must keep eyes and ears open, drawing material from all walks of life—observation is an ongoing, essential source of power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a writer 'shuts his eyes and shuts his ears' (ceases observing) the work deteriorates. Observation should be unconscious and continuous in all movements and intercourse with others; losing this leads to stale writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasing the reader is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer of stories must please; without pleasing the reader the novelist fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope states bluntly 'The writer of stories must please, or he will be nothing.' This is not mere entertainment: pleasure is the vehicle by which teaching and ethical aims can be effectively communicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach through narrative; make virtue attractive and vice ugly
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist with conscience should instruct ethically by showing consequences in the story, making virtue alluring and vice repellent, rather than using blunt sermons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novels should 'preach his sermons' as a clergyman does but through character and plot. Trollope cites Miss Edgeworth, Austen, Scott, Thackeray, Dickens, and George Eliot as doing this effectively; characters who err should be shown as dishonoured rather than simply punished with explicit moralizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth of description and character (human truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction must exhibit truth in description and in the portrayal of character—human truth is foundational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without truth of description and human truth the reader cannot sympathize. Trollope argues this truth is what makes scenes, whether comic or tragic, succeed and what allows a reader to feel the characters are 'flesh and blood.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Create sympathetic, believable characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters must be realised so readers can sympathize with them; sympathy is necessary for comedy or tragedy to work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples invoked include Rebecca, Burley, the mad lady in Jane Eyre, Lady Castlewood, Lady Mason. If characters are not people we can sympathise with, emotional effects fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine realism and sensationalism where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: A good novel should be both realistic (character and detail) and sensational (an engaging, developed plot); failure in either is a failure in art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope rejects the binary dividing authors and readers into 'sensational' vs 'realistic'—the best work attains both. He notes limitations of imperfect artists who cannot achieve both and recommends striving for the highest degree of each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure sensational elements arise from character and truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational or horrific incidents must be grounded in known, believable persons and arise naturally from character and situation; avoid sensationalism for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: piling horrors that are not tied to real persons or character results in dull, useless fiction (he gives the absurd example of endless, disconnected murders). Sensational incidents should move from and illuminate character, not exist as mere shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle love responsibly as a central novel element
rubrics_metrics.description: Because love commonly motivates novels and reaches a wide readership (especially the young), it should be portrayed to teach wholesome expectations and conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope argues love can teach young readers valuable lessons if handled properly (e.g. Laura Bell and Pendennis). He disputes the idea that hearing about love before marriage necessarily corrupts; instead, novels can promote honest, desirable notions of love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid glamorising borderline immoral behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of the 'borderlands' of vice where alluring descriptions can make immoral behavior attractive; do not sacrifice moral clarity for effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope warns that outskirts of absolute vice have 'sweet-smelling flowers' and are dangerous—novelists may be tempted to depict alluring borderline immorality for effect. Instead, ensure such portrayals lead readers to reject such behaviour (e.g. Beatrix shown as attractive yet dishonourable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid writing from habit or commercial pressure (don't become a trade)
rubrics_metrics.description: After success some writers produce books from habit or obligation rather than fresh observation, causing weakening of art; resist becoming merely a trade.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symptoms include characters as 'wooden blocks', palpably arranged incidents, and a mechanical course of the tale. Trollope notes many great writers have suffered this decline when their work became routine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure plotting shows natural cause-and-effect (avoid stiff mechanism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot construction should make events appear necessary consequences of prior actions and character, not merely arranged mechanical incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should feel 'only for that flame of the eye, only for that angry word ... all might have been different.' If the plot is a visible mechanism, the work feels artificial and fails to engage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and critically to understand the art of the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Study the history and range of novels extensively to be able to point out excellences and defects—intensive, critical reading informs good practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope describes his aborted project to write a history of English prose fiction and the necessity of reading an 'infinity of novels' so as to read some 'so as to point out the excellences' and explain defects. He recommends indefatigable, light-handed study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise the social influence and responsibility of novels
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels shape expectations and behavior (what girls and young men learn about love, ambition, honesty); writers bear responsibility for the effects of their portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trollope explains novels teach a 'vast proportion of the teaching of the day'—authors should be conscience-driven about how characters' actions model behavior, since readers (especially the young) may imitate what fiction portrays as leading to 'glorious' results.
